common_name: Tiger Eyes Sumac (Golden Cutleaf Staghorn Sumac)

planting.note: Plant container-grown, grafted specimens in well-drained, average to poor soil in partial shade to full sun in spring or fall; because Tiger Eyes is grafted onto straight-species rootstock, remove any green-leaved suckers that arise below the graft union, since they will overtake the golden scion if left to grow.

directions: Tiger Eyes is a compact sport of staghorn sumac selected for deeply cut, lacy, fern-like foliage that emerges chartreuse-yellow in spring, holds bright gold through summer on contrasting pink-red leaf stalks, then finishes with fiery orange-scarlet fall color, giving three seasons of striking foliage color on a shrub roughly half the size of the wild species. It still spreads by root suckers to form a colony over time, though far less aggressively than the species, and its fuzzy, cone-shaped red berry clusters persist into winter and feed birds. Give it some afternoon shade in hot climates, since the pale gold leaves scorch more readily than green foliage in intense summer sun; this cultivar is best suited to cooler regions and can struggle with the combination of extreme heat and humidity found deep in the Gulf South.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox
Chicagoland Grows / First Editions Plant Introduction Program

common_name: Gro-Low Fragrant Sumac (Dwarf Spreading Groundcover Sumac)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in well-drained, average to poor, dry soil in full sun to partial shade in spring or fall; Gro-Low tolerates infertile, compacted, or eroding soil that few other groundcover shrubs handle well, and roots readily where trailing stems touch the ground.

directions: Gro-Low is a low, wide-spreading selection of native fragrant sumac grown as a tough, drought-tolerant groundcover for slopes, parking lot islands, and other difficult dry sites where turf struggles. Its glossy, three-lobed leaflets resemble poison ivy in outline but are harmless and release a spicy, citrus-like fragrance when crushed; small yellow flower clusters in early spring are followed by fuzzy red berries and then a reliable orange-to-burgundy fall color display. Once established it needs no supplemental irrigation, spreads steadily by rooting where branches touch soil to form a dense, weed-suppressing mat, and requires only an occasional hard pruning in late winter to keep it within bounds.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

common_name: Lemony Lace Elderberry (Golden Cutleaf Ornamental Elderberry)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; give Lemony Lace some afternoon shade in hot climates, where its bright gold foliage is prone to scorch in full, reflected summer sun.

directions: Lemony Lace is a compact, rounded ornamental elderberry selected for finely dissected, lacy, bright chartreuse-gold foliage held on contrasting near-black stems, a dramatic color and texture combination for a mixed border or foundation planting. Flat clusters of pinkish-white flowers appear in late spring, followed by small red berries that, like other red elderberries, are mildly toxic raw and should be cooked before any culinary use, or simply left for birds. It stays noticeably smaller and denser than wild red elderberry, needs only light shaping after bloom, and performs best where summers are not extremely hot and humid, since foliage color and vigor decline in the most intense Deep South heat.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container roses in early spring or fall in slightly acidic, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Pink Double Knock Out shares the disease resistance and repeat bloom of the rest of the Knock Out family but carries fully double, ruffled flowers rather than the single five-petaled blooms of the original.

directions: Pink Double Knock Out combines the legendary disease resistance and near-continuous rebloom of the Knock Out rose family with a fuller, more traditionally rose-shaped flower, carrying densely petaled, medium-pink, ruffled double blooms instead of the simple five-petaled flowers of the original red Knock Out. Like its relatives it is essentially self-cleaning, dropping spent petals cleanly without deadheading, and shows outstanding natural resistance to black spot and powdery mildew in the humid Gulf South. It blooms in flushes from spring through frost and needs only a hard prune to 12-18 inches in late winter to renew vigorous flowering growth for the coming season; avoid planting in less than a full six hours of direct sun, which reduces bloom significantly.
sources: Star Roses and Plants — Knock Out Rose Family

common_name: Blushing Knock Out Rose (Pale Pink Knock Out)

planting.note: Plant container roses in early spring or fall in slightly acidic, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Blushing Knock Out's pale coloring makes it a versatile mixer in pastel plantings while retaining the full disease resistance and repeat bloom of the Knock Out family.

directions: Blushing Knock Out is the softest-colored member of the Knock Out rose family, carrying single, five-petaled flowers in a pale, blush pink that is noticeably lighter than the medium-pink of Pink Knock Out, giving it a delicate, old-fashioned look at a distance despite being just as tough as its relatives up close. It shares the same essentially disease-immune performance against black spot and powdery mildew, self-cleaning habit that drops spent flowers without deadheading, and continuous bloom cycle from spring through frost in zone 9. Prune the entire plant back hard, to 12-18 inches, in late winter to encourage strong new growth and maximize the coming season's bloom, and provide a full six hours or more of direct sun for the best flower production.
sources: Star Roses and Plants — Knock Out Rose Family
